title: Sprint 3 — DB Schema: Data Modeling with DBML
description: Design normalized schemas, establish primary and foreign key constraints, enforce uniqueness, and model relational data structures using DBML.

tickets.title: Design a URL Mapping Database
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Design the relational database schema in DBML for a URL shortener, ensuring unique alias lookups and tracking click analytics.

### Primary Tab
**DB Schema · DBML**

### Requirements
1. Create a `urls` table with primary key, original URL, short code, and timestamps.
2. Enforce a unique constraint on `short_code` to prevent collisions.
3. Create a `url_clicks` analytics table referencing `urls.id` via foreign key.
4. Design appropriate indexes for O(1) redirection lookups.

### Acceptance Criteria
- DBML schema enforces uniqueness on short codes and defines valid relationships between URLs and analytics entries.
tasks: Create a `urls` table with primary key, original URL, short code, and created_at timestamp.
Enforce uniqueness on the short code column (`[unique]`).
Create a `url_clicks` table with a foreign key referencing `urls.id` (`[ref: > urls.id]`).
Document an indexing strategy for fast short code resolution.
learning_objectives: Learn DBML syntax for tables, column types, and constraints (`[pk]`, `[unique]`, `[ref]`).
Design 1-to-many relationships with foreign key integrity.
Choose appropriate column data types for URLs, hashes, and timestamps.
common_mistakes: Omitting the unique constraint on the short code column.
Using unbounded or inefficient string types for hashes.
Failing to relate click analytics to parent URL records.
hints: In DBML: `Table urls { id bigint [pk] short_code varchar [unique] ... }`.
Establish foreign key using `ref: > urls.id` inside the child table column definition.
Include counters or analytics tracking tables.

system_design.schema:
Table urls {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  short_code varchar(10) [unique, not null]
  original_url text [not null]
  created_by bigint
  click_count bigint [default: 0]
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
  expires_at timestamp
}

Table url_clicks {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  url_id bigint [ref: > urls.id, not null]
  ip_hash varchar(64)
  country_code varchar(3)
  user_agent text
  clicked_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

notes.schema:
## URL Mapping Data Model
- `urls`: Stores short codes with unique B-tree index for O(1) redirection lookup.
- `url_clicks`: Tracks every redirect access with foreign key to parent URL.
- High-velocity click logs can be partitioned or aggregated into daily metrics.

solution.explanation: Defines relational schema with primary/foreign keys, uniqueness constraints on the short code, and an audit table for click telemetry.
solution.approach: Normalized DBML schema with foreign key relationships.

tickets.title: Design an E-commerce Database
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Design the relational database schema in DBML for an e-commerce platform supporting users, product catalog, orders, and order line items.

### Primary Tab
**DB Schema · DBML**

### Requirements
1. Create `users`, `products`, `orders`, and `order_items` tables.
2. Define primary keys (`[pk]`) and foreign keys (`[ref: > ...]`).
3. Model the many-to-many relationship between orders and products via the `order_items` join table.
4. Preserve historical purchase price inside `order_items` so future product price changes do not alter past orders.

### Acceptance Criteria
- Schema preserves historical pricing integrity and establishes valid relational constraints.
tasks: Create `users`, `products`, `orders`, and `order_items` tables.
Define primary keys and foreign key relationships between orders, users, and products.
Model the many-to-many relationship through `order_items`.
Store historical `unit_price` on `order_items` to protect order history integrity.
learning_objectives: Model many-to-many relationships through associative join entities.
Understand temporal data integrity: snapshotting prices at transaction time.
Define decimal types for currency and status enumerations.
common_mistakes: Referencing `products.price` directly for past orders instead of storing historical price in `order_items`.
Omitting foreign keys on `order_items` to `orders` and `products`.
Using float instead of decimal for financial currencies.
hints: `order_items` needs `order_id bigint [ref: > orders.id]` and `product_id bigint [ref: > products.id]`.

system_design.schema:
Table users {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  email varchar(255) [unique, not null]
  password_hash varchar(255) [not null]
  full_name varchar(150)
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table products {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  sku varchar(50) [unique, not null]
  name varchar(255) [not null]
  description text
  price decimal(10,2) [not null]
  stock_quantity int [not null, default: 0]
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table orders {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  user_id bigint [ref: > users.id, not null]
  status varchar(30) [not null, default: 'PENDING']
  total_amount decimal(10,2) [not null]
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table order_items {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  order_id bigint [ref: > orders.id, not null]
  product_id bigint [ref: > products.id, not null]
  unit_price decimal(10,2) [not null]
  quantity int [not null, default: 1]
}

notes.schema:
## E-commerce Data Model Decisions
- `order_items.unit_price` snapshots the purchase price at time of order creation.
- Decimal precision (10,2) prevents floating-point rounding errors on currency calculations.
- Relational foreign keys maintain referential integrity.

solution.explanation: Accurately represents relational e-commerce tables, junction table constraints, and pricing snapshot preservation.
solution.approach: Third Normal Form (3NF) relational design with historical price snapshotting.

tickets.title: Design a Notification Database
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Design the relational database schema in DBML for a multi-channel notification platform (Email, SMS, Push) that tracks delivery attempts, templates, and statuses.

### Primary Tab
**DB Schema · DBML**

### Requirements
1. Create `notification_templates`, `notifications`, and `notification_attempts` tables.
2. Define statuses: `PENDING`, `PROCESSING`, `SENT`, `FAILED`.
3. Establish foreign keys linking delivery attempts to their parent notification.
4. Design schema to track error messages, provider responses, and timestamps for every delivery retry.

### Acceptance Criteria
- Multiple delivery attempts can be tracked and audited per notification request.
tasks: Create `notification_templates`, `notifications`, and `notification_attempts` tables.
Define status columns with states: PENDING, SENT, FAILED.
Relate delivery attempts to parent notifications (`[ref: > notifications.id]`).
Include provider response and error message columns on attempts for observability.
learning_objectives: Design audit log tables for asynchronous background jobs.
Model reusable template configurations with variable interpolation.
Track parent-child execution attempts for distributed workflows.
common_mistakes: Overwriting previous delivery attempt errors instead of logging each retry row.
Hardcoding templates in application code rather than a dedicated database entity.
Missing foreign key constraints between notifications and attempts.
hints: Create a 1-to-many relationship: One `notifications` row has many `notification_attempts` rows.
Store the template key on `notification_templates` with a unique constraint.
Record attempt number, provider name, and error response on `notification_attempts`.

system_design.schema:
Table notification_templates {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  template_key varchar(100) [unique, not null]
  channel varchar(30) [not null]
  subject text
  body_template text [not null]
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table notifications {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  user_id bigint [not null]
  template_id bigint [ref: > notification_templates.id]
  channel varchar(30) [not null]
  status varchar(30) [not null, default: 'PENDING']
  recipient text [not null]
  payload_json text
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table notification_attempts {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  notification_id bigint [ref: > notifications.id, not null]
  attempt_number int [not null]
  provider_name varchar(50) [not null]
  status varchar(30) [not null]
  error_message text
  response_code int
  attempted_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

notes.schema:
## Notification Audit Schema
- Every retry is appended as a new row in `notification_attempts`.
- Preserves complete operational history for debugging provider deliverability.
- Decouples template rendering from notification execution.

solution.explanation: Separates notification intent from execution attempts, enabling full auditability and retry tracking.
solution.approach: Parent-child event audit log data modeling in DBML.

tickets.title: Design a Multi-tenant SaaS Database
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Design the relational database schema in DBML for a multi-tenant B2B SaaS platform (like GitHub or Linear) where users can join multiple organizations with distinct roles.

### Primary Tab
**DB Schema · DBML**

### Requirements
1. Create `organizations`, `users`, `memberships`, and `projects` tables.
2. Model users belonging to multiple organizations through a `memberships` table.
3. Enforce membership roles (`ADMIN`, `MEMBER`, `VIEWER`) and uniqueness on `(org_id, user_id)`.
4. Ensure all tenant-owned entities (e.g. `projects`) have an explicit foreign key to `organizations.id` for row-level security.

### Acceptance Criteria
- Schema enforces tenant isolation and supports many-to-many user-organization memberships.
tasks: Create `organizations`, `users`, `memberships`, and `projects` tables in DBML.
Model users belonging to multiple organizations via `memberships`.
Define membership roles and uniqueness constraints (`unique(org_id, user_id)`).
Ensure tenant-owned records link directly to `organizations.id` for strict tenant isolation.
learning_objectives: Master multi-tenant shared-database row-level tenant separation.
Design Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) membership schemas.
Prevent cross-tenant data leakage through explicit foreign keys.
common_mistakes: Hardcoding an `org_id` on the `users` table, preventing users from joining multiple organizations.
Omitting tenant foreign keys on subsidiary resource tables like `projects`.
Failing to enforce unique constraints on membership pairings.
hints: `memberships` table should have `org_id [ref: > organizations.id]` and `user_id [ref: > users.id]`.
`projects` must have `org_id [ref: > organizations.id]` to enforce tenant boundary.

system_design.schema:
Table organizations {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  slug varchar(100) [unique, not null]
  name varchar(255) [not null]
  plan varchar(50) [default: 'FREE']
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table users {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  email varchar(255) [unique, not null]
  full_name varchar(150)
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table memberships {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  org_id bigint [ref: > organizations.id, not null]
  user_id bigint [ref: > users.id, not null]
  role varchar(30) [not null, default: 'MEMBER']
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table projects {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  org_id bigint [ref: > organizations.id, not null]
  name varchar(255) [not null]
  status varchar(30) [default: 'ACTIVE']
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

notes.schema:
## Multi-tenant Schema Architecture
- Row-level multitenancy: `org_id` partitioned on every tenant entity.
- `memberships` associative entity allows a single user login to access multiple companies.
- Prevents data crossover using strict composite indexes and foreign key references.

solution.explanation: Implements row-level multi-tenancy with an associative membership model supporting RBAC roles across organizations.
solution.approach: Row-level multi-tenant database design with RBAC memberships.

tickets.title: Design a Ticket Booking Database
tickets.description:
### Scenario
Design the relational database schema in DBML for a high-concurrency event booking platform (like Ticketmaster or BookMyShow) that manages seat reservations, payment holds, and concurrency safety.

### Primary Tab
**DB Schema · DBML**

### Requirements
1. Create `events`, `seats`, `bookings`, and `payments` tables.
2. Model temporary seat holds with `status` (`HELD`, `CONFIRMED`, `CANCELLED`, `EXPIRED`) and an `expires_at` timestamp.
3. Prevent duplicate active bookings for the same seat using unique constraints.
4. Link payments to bookings with transaction ID and status tracking.

### Acceptance Criteria
- Schema reliably supports concurrency-safe seat allocation, expiration timestamps, and payment tracking.
tasks: Create `events`, `seats`, `bookings`, and `payments` tables in DBML.
Model temporary seat holds with status and `expires_at` timestamp columns.
Establish foreign key relationships connecting seats to events, bookings to seats, and payments to bookings.
Design constraints to prevent simultaneous active bookings for the same seat.
learning_objectives: Model state machine lifecycles (Held -> Confirmed -> Expired) in database schemas.
Design temporal expiration fields for transaction timeouts.
Enforce data integrity under high-concurrency reservation scenarios.
common_mistakes: Omitting the expiration timestamp (`expires_at`) for temporary reservations.
Failing to track payment transaction references.
Allowing multiple confirmed booking records for the same seat.
hints: `bookings` table links to `seats.id` and has an `expires_at timestamp`.

system_design.schema:
Table events {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  title varchar(255) [not null]
  venue varchar(255) [not null]
  starts_at timestamp [not null]
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table seats {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  event_id bigint [ref: > events.id, not null]
  section varchar(50) [not null]
  seat_number varchar(20) [not null]
  price decimal(10,2) [not null]
}

Table bookings {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  user_id bigint [not null]
  seat_id bigint [ref: > seats.id, not null]
  status varchar(30) [not null, default: 'HELD']
  expires_at timestamp [not null]
  created_at timestamp [default: `now()`]
}

Table payments {
  id bigint [pk, increment]
  booking_id bigint [ref: > bookings.id, not null]
  transaction_id varchar(100) [unique, not null]
  amount decimal(10,2) [not null]
  status varchar(30) [not null]
  paid_at timestamp
}

notes.schema:
## Ticket Booking Schema Design
- `bookings.expires_at`: Enforces hard TTL for seat holds (e.g. 10 minutes).
- Status values: 'HELD' -> 'CONFIRMED' or 'EXPIRED'.
- Unique constraint prevents duplicate active holds per seat.

solution.explanation: Models seat hold states, TTL expiration timestamps, and payment tracking for concurrency-safe event bookings.
solution.approach: Stateful reservation entity with temporal TTL fields.
